=== FILE: 4 minutes to fix your BUM SHOULDERS! [_TFQi2kVRoM].txt ===

try this shoulder and upper back progression next time you plan on putting a barbell overhead, squatting it, or if you plan on front squatting it, especially if you plan on front squatting it. This exercise progression involves kettlebell shoulder presses, kettlebell overhead squats, and a kettlebell SOTS press. A SOTS press is an overhead press from the bottom of a squat, popularized by a Russian weightlifter named Victor SOTS. It's always the Eastern European guys who get to name these exercises. I was inspired to create this exercise progression that I've been using for a couple of months now. I created it, patent pending. I was inspired by Dan John, listening to him talk about how he views the shoulders as having individual suspension, which is just a fun kind of quirky way of saying that if you are prone to shoulder issues when you press a barbell overhead or when you press a fixed machine, try doing some unilateral work with dumbbells or kettlebells, one arm presses, so that each shoulder and each arm can move independently. I have five levels for this progression because five is a perfect number. I would suggest doing four to eight reps per arm at each of these levels. Level one is a standing alternating kettlebell press. I like to start with the kettlebells under my chin, sort of in front of my body, and then one at a time I'll press and rotate the kettlebell to lock out directly over my shoulder joint. I like to think about having my bicep in line with my ears at the top. I'll do a couple of sets with ascending kettlebell weights until I feel like I'm using an appropriate amount of weight. Level two, standing alternating kettlebell press with offhand up. This is the same as level one, except now the offhand doesn't get a break. It has to stabilize at the top while the other hand performs its rep. Level three, a one-armed overhead squat. With the kettlebell in one hand, press overhead and then perform a deep squat. You're probably going to need to place your heels on some sort of raised surface, like a plate, some wedges, or even just at the edge of a platform. The overhead squat places a huge demand on your upper back, forcing you to extend it as best as you can. If you have a naturally kyphotic posture or a rounded upper back, this is going to be very difficult. Just do your best. Many people blame a poor overhead position for lack of shoulder mobility, when oftentimes it's a rounded upper back that's to blame. Level four, a one-armed SOTS press. Now you're going to produce some force at the bottom of a squat, which is a less than ideal position to do so. Just like the standing one-armed overhead press, I like to rotate the kettlebell as I press, holding each lockout for one second. You can perform this with one kettlebell at a time, or do a wielding with two kettlebells, alternating sides. Level five, a double kettlebell SOTS press. At the bottom of a squat, press both kettlebells to lockout simultaneously. When you press one kettlebell, you have freedom to twist your body in order to reach lockout. You don't have that freedom when both arms are pressing simultaneously. This demands full extension of your upper back and full flexion of your shoulders. Now you don't need to be at level five today. Work your way up to whatever level you're comfortable with. Stay there as long as you need to. You could use dumbbells for this instead of kettlebells. I just like the way the kettlebell feels, because when the kettlebell's in my hand, the weight is behind my wrist, and so that pulls my arm back into a better position when it's overhead. You can perform this progression as often as you'd like, especially if it's really light at first. It's not going to be very stressful. Do it a few times a week. One thing I really like about this progression is that it doesn't feel like a waste of time. It doesn't feel like I'm in a physical therapy rehab setting doing some really silly corrective exercises that don't really stress me. These can be hard. These can be heavy. I can use this as a workout rather than thinking of it as prehab or rehab exercises. I can load this progressively over time. That's it. Thanks for watching. And always remember, tren on time.

Hey everyone, I'm Alan Thrall here at home because it fits the theme of today's video. I'm going to outline a very simple basic program for individuals starting from scratch, ground zero, probably below ground zero. The demographic that I'm targetinGHere, elderly, morbidly obese, overweight, sick, maybe someone who's recently hospitalized, anyone who's severely undertrened. This program might be for you or a client, family member, loved one. It is meant to be done at home, although it can be done in a gym. There's no equipment needed other than a rope, a strap, a towel, or a band to hold onto. This program is designed to increase physical independence, improve strength, balanced coordination, and confidence. Box squats. These are for the legs. Place feet around shoulder width with toes pointing out around 10 and two o'clock. Grab a towel, a strong strap, or a band and wrap it around a sturdy post. Here, I'm just using a tie down ratchet strap that I got out of my truck. Squat down to the box by pushing your knees out and sitting your hips back and down to the box or the chair. Try not to collapse on the box. Pause, stand back up. The towel, band, or strap is there to allow you to use your arms for assistance if needed. Over time, use less and less arms, eventually doing squats without your hands. Focus on keeping your feet flat as you squat down and stand up. Inclined push-ups. This is for the upper body. Find a sturdy, elevated surface. Place your hands just outside of shoulder width. While keeping your body straight, lower yourself until your chest touches the surface. Press your body back up. The higher the surface and the more vertical your body is, the easier the press will be. The lower the surface and the more horizontal your body is, the more difficult the press will be. Knee lifts. This is for abs. Stand to the side of a post. Grab the post for balance. Repeatedly lift one knee as high as you can. Switch sides. Take your hand off the post once you're comfortable. Toes to sky touches. This is for your back and upper body. Stand with your feet hip width. Bend over and try to touch your toes. Stand up and immediately reach your hands to the sky. Use any items you can find around the house to add resistance. Step-ups. This is for legs and balance. Find a short, elevated surface such as a stair. Place your hands at your hips or against the wall. Step up one leg at a time, keeping the front foot flat. Perform all reps on one leg, then switch to the other leg. Rope inverted row. Find a stable overhead beam or a sturdy tree branch. Wrap a reliable strap around the beam or branch. While keeping your body straight, lower yourself and perform two-handed inverted rows. Similar to the push-ups, the more vertical you are, the easier the row is. The more horizontal you are, the more difficult the row is. Perform anywhere between 10 to 20 reps for each exercise, 2 to 5 total sets. That's it. Thanks for watching and always remember, TRINITYME!

=== FILE: Goals Are Wildly Overrated [GOP9oaHmvrs].txt ===

if you don't have a goal, what's the point? Going to the gym without a goal is the best way to get nowhere. Working out in the gym without a goal is just exercise. It's not trening. These are all things that I've heard said. I'm sure you've heard them said as well. And I used to just kind of shake my head in agreement until recently, maybe I had a change of heart. I heard someone say that and they said, if you don't have a goal, what's the point? And my face twisted up in disagreement. If you don't have any set goals for yourself, that is okay. Going to the gym is still a productive thing to do. Even if you don't have goals, I'm not going to sit here and cover the physical, mental, emotional, psychological benefits of exercise. So saying, you know, what's the point of being in the gym if you don't have goals is a nonsensical thing to say. Now I'm not here to bash on goals and I'm not telling you that goals are meaningless, useless, or a waste of time. If you like setting goals for yourself and if having goals keeps you consistent in the gym, if you need that direction, if you need something to chase, that's totally fine. More power to you, set all the goals you want. But if you can't figure out your goals, don't just make them up because someone, you know, pressured you into it. You can go to the gym and have direction and purpose without having specific goals. You can just pick exercises based on what you enjoy doing, what feels good, what motivates you, what excites you, picking things that you look forward to doing, doing things that you feel offer the greatest benefits. And by doing that, you are still reaping the same rewards from exercise as someone, you know, who has specific goals in mind. I'm not saying that goals are wildly overrated just because I'm trying to be contrarian. It's just that all too often, especially in my circle, I see people sign up for competitions because they think that they need to, you know, what's the point of trening if you don't have a comp to prep for, right? And they will drag themselves through four months of trening for competition prep and they hate most of those four months and they complain about the struggles of competition prep. Maybe they accomplish their goal or even surpass their weight loss goal, but then they just end up rebounding back in body weight once it's over. === FILE: How & Why You Should SUPERSET Your Exercises [hU3Np33jud4].txt ===

Hey everyone, I'm Alan Thorall here at Untamed Strength Gym in Sacramento, California, and in this video I'm going to be talking about supersets. A superset is when you take two exercises, perform them back to back for one consecutive set, one big set, one superset. For example, you might do 10 bicep curls followed immediately by 10 tricep press downs. That's one superset. You would rest and then perform your second superset. If you were to do two exercises, three sets of each exercise done as a superset, it would look like this here, how you see on the screen. Back in April of this year, I started following a program by Natural Hypertrophy who utilizes supersets exclusively. Every exercise is supersetted with another exercise, at least in this program in particular, and I got to say that I am hooked. I really, really like it, and I want to share with you some benefits, but most notably, some considerations to make before incorporating supersets for yourself. The concept of supersets is not new to me. However, my implementation was different. When I did use supersets, I did it as a way to make things more difficult, to increase the suck factor. So IMight superset something like barbell squats and squat jumps, goblet squats, superset with lunges, bench press, superset pushups, deadlifts, superset back extensions, rows, superset band pull-aparts. So I want you to take a second to think, what about these supersets, these exercises stands out to you? That's right, each exercise is working the same muscle groups, or at least the same patterns back-to-back. This makes each set much more difficult than if you were to separate the sets and do them on their own with a rest period in between each set. Doing supersets like this does have value, particularly for sports performance. Squatting, followed immediately by running, followed by jumping, performed back-to-back-to-back might have value if you're trening for basketball, or if you're a football player. Doing deadlifts, rows, and back extensions might be good if you are a strongman competitor, because you are going to have to prepare yourself for 90 seconds of continuous work, 90 second medleys where you do deadlifts for reps, followed immediately by farmer's carry, followed by a keg carry, all of this stuff back-to-back-to-back. You need to, your trening needs to push the limits of lactic acid threshold. Crossfitters need the endurance to perform similar movements back-to-back. For example, deadlifts and rower, handstand push-ups, and medicine ball overhead throws. So supersetting two exercises working the same muscle groups might help you if your goal is to build endurance for sports performance, but if you're not interested in that and you just want to build some muscle or strength, there's a better, more efficient way to incorporate and implement supersets into your routine. Two exercises done as a superset will always be opposing muscle groups or antagonistic muscle groups. The most obvious example would be biceps and triceps. The bicep controls elbow flexion, the tricep controls elbow extension. So it makes sense to group these together and superset these movements. You could also think about antagonistic movement patterns. So a vertical press, like an overhead press, superset with a vertical pull, like a pull-up or a lat pull-down. A horizontal press, like a bench press or a push-up, supersetted with a horizontal pull, like a dumbbell row or a chest supported row. Knee extension, like a leg extension machine, superset with knee flexion, a hamstring leg curl machine. These supersets don't always have to be big compound movements superset with other big compound movements or smaller isolation movements supersetted only with smaller isolation movements. You could do that, but you can also mix and match. So you might think, well squats work my quads and Romanian deadlifts work my hamstrings. Boom, perfect superset. It might be a good superset on paper, but in practice it's incredibly difficult to maintain a high level of performance or a high level of effort with two very big taxing compound movements. Personally I enjoy supersetting big compound movements like squats and deadlifts with smaller flexion movements like neck flexion or abs. Squats and deadlifts are knee extension, hip extension movements. You're trying to stand up, whereas ab trening is a hip flexion movement. So these two movements work well together and doing abs or neck in between my sets of squats is no sweat off my brow. Doing ab work does not affect my leg work at all. Supersets are also a great way to add frequency of smaller movements because they can be added to any available slot throughout the week. Now I've already mentioned neck flexion and neck extension, so I'll use those as an example. These movements in particular can be superset with any other movement throughout the week. You could also add calves, arms, or you know maybe forearms throughout your weekly routine without it negatively affecting the other movements that you're supersetting it with. Rather than trying to lump together all of that trening onto two days, maybe just two upper body days, you could spread that out to three days a week or maybe even to four days per week. I superset Romanian deadlifts with dumbbell lateral raises which seem sort of odd, hamstrings and shoulders, but it actually makes sense if you think about it. When I'm doing a Romanian deadlift there is some shoulder extension happening because I'm trying to keep the bar close to my body. I'm using my lats to prevent it from swinging out away from me and as I come up I am pulling the bar close to my body to get some more lat engagement. So there's some shoulder extension happening and then I would superset that with a form of shoulder flexion raising my arm. It's more abduction doing a dumbbell lateral raise. Those terms don't matter. What I'm saying is they sync well together. Supersetting will save you time in the gym, but that's actually not its sole purpose. IMake a lot of content about saving time in the gym, but truth be told doing supersets is not going to take two hours of work and magically condense it down into 30 minutes of work. Supersets, however, will allow you to get more work done in the same amount of time and that's within your daily routine or even your weekly routine. If you're trying to do 10 to 20 sets per body part per week or if you're more of a strength focused person and you focus more on sets of movement per week, let's say you do 8 to 12 sets of squats, bench and deadlift per week. If each of those sets has its own rest period, its own three to four five minute rest period, it's going to take a long time. By supersetting you can cut your total rest time for a trening session or in a week by half at most. More realistically I would guess you'd cut your rest time by about a third. Beyond that, a time-saving benefit to supersets and giant sets is increased focus. If I'm performing exercise A and then exercise B and then I'm resting for a short period of time thinking about my next set of exercise A, I don't get bored. I don't lose focus. If I sit down for five minutes after a set of squats, especially if I have my phone nearby, I'm going to get distracted. I'm going to lose my focus. Supersets keep me engaged in the entire workout. Now there are no hard rules to supersetting. You can organize and structure your routine however you want based on your own preferred split or maybe equipment availability in your gym. Also the layout of your gym. There are times when I'll lump together two exercises just because it's easy to do both exercises in the same rack or in the same spot of the gym. I won't do a superset if it's on this side of the gym and way over here on that side of the gym if the gym's busy so I can structure it accordingly. For instance, right now I've been doing decline dumbbell skull crushers. As soon as I'm done with my set I'll drop the bells and I'll do decline sit-ups. Seamless trensition. The only rule I would follow is to not group together two exercises if there's a noticeable drop in performance on either of those exercises. I'm not going to superset my squats and deadlifts. I'm not going to superset atlas stone loads and barbell clen and press for obvious reasons. People who are skeptical of supersets, first off you don't have to if you don't want to, but they'll often say that they are worried they're going to be winded if they don't have a dedicated three, four, or five minutes after each working set. Yes, if you are very out of shape there's going to be a noticeable drop in performance once you start doing supersets, but if you really want to get better, if you really want to get in shape, like anything you'll adapt if you stick to it for long enough. I would argue that for myself supersetting my exercises saves energy and it increases performance. Crazy, I know. So when I get to the gym I have this running internal clock. After about 90 minutes my energy starts to dwindle a bit, my focus starts to slip, my excitement to tren has slightly worn off, and I'm just ready to switch gears and move on because I'm sorry but I got to do. So let's say this was my workout. I had three rounds of overhead press superset with pull-ups, three rounds of dips superset with dumbbell rows, and three rounds of dumbbell curls superset dumbbell french press. I'm just making this workout up. If I eliminated the supersets and I separated everything I would switch from nine supersets to 18 total sets. It's the same amount of total work but the 18 sets would obviously take much longer. Supersets allow me to get more work in, they keep me engaged and focused, they keep my effort at tip-top quality. Maybe they'll do the same for you. That's it, thanks for watching and always remember, tren ON!

If it means something to you, that's a good enough reason to chase it. With that out of the way, I'm just going to focus on the three primary reasons that I listed. Being strong makes physical aspects of life easier, makes you more durable, helps you live longer. What does it mean to be physically strong? Let's say someone deadlifts 405 pounds. Most would call that strong, but that person can't do three pull-ups. Someone else can do 20 strict pull-ups, but can't bench 225 pounds. Someone can farmers carry 75% of their body weight in each hand for a quarter mile, but can't deadlift two times their body weight for one rep. Most people watching this video, most people in my circle of fitness often default to the barbell when talking about strength standards and for good reason. I've talked about at length why barbells are awesome for building strength. Go search any of my videos from 2016 to 2019. That's pretty much all I talked about. Barbell movements are a great strength builder and a great strength tester. They can be incrementally loaded, heavier than we would ever need, making them great for progression. They can be trened through a full range of motion, and they tren a lot of muscle mass. These paraphrased reasons are from the Starting Strength book, and in my opinion, they're pretty sound reasons to use a barbell. So barbells are great, and honestly, most strength standard recommendations you find online are reasonable. Strength standards like the thousand pound club, one, two, three, four plate press bench squat deadlift. I'm fine with any of those, but are barbells the only metric we can use to define physical strength? What if someone decided to pursue bodyweight trening only for the rest of their life? What if someone decided to pursue machine hypertrophy trening for the rest of their life? Would these people have a lower quality of life? Would their expected lifespan be shorter? I'm going to assume no and no. Take a look at Daniel from Fitness FAQ. He's primarily a calisthenics guy who recently made a video showing that he can't bench press 100 kilograms, 220 pounds. This dude can do weighted dips and pull-ups for reps with 40 kilos, 50 kilos, maybe 60 kilos. I don't even know. Take a look at natural bodybuilder Jeff Alberts. Jeff is in his 50s, and I really never see him do back squats, deadlifts, and bench press with a barbell. Do you think he would improve his quality of life, durability, and lifespan if he just started focusing on improvinGHis barbell squat, deadlift, and bench press? Again, no. And they might acquire some minor injuries if they started to specialize for squat, bench, deadlift max strength. Take a look at Max, a guy on Instagram who goes by the handle BusyDadtrening. He primarily does minimalist trening with burpees and bodyweight exercises. This dude is in phenomenal shape. Do you think he should worry about his bench press to bodyweight ratio? Should he start worrying about gettinGHis squat up to three plates? He could live a happy, healthy, strong life never touching a barbell, or even weights for that matter. Seeing these examples proves to me that strength can be expressed in many ways, following many routines, using a variety of different metrics. And this is one reason why it's hard for me to give barbell strength standards, or to answer thEQuestion, how strong is strong enough? People fall into the trap of thinking barbell strength is the most important physical attribute. I know I did at one point. They'll avoid conditioning because it might affect their strength. They'll gain an unhealthy amount of bodyweight to facilitate weight increases on the bar. They'll drag themselves through chronic aches and pains in pursuit of PRs. They'll become frustrated and dissatisfied when their numbers aren't improving, never really appreciating the progress that's behind them, all while probably being strong enough. Sometimes the number one thing that a person needs to make themselves harder to kill is to lose about 60 pounds of bodyweight, even if that means they lose 120 pounds on their barbell squat. A heart attack doesn't care if you squat 455 pounds. Your elevated blood pressure is not waiting for you to increase your bench press from 290 to 305 pounds. Some people would be a stronger, healthier, more physically capable person by getting their mile time under 10 minutes, not by killing themselves trying to bring their deadlift from 395 to 405. I still receive comments about my weight loss that was from six years ago now. People still say, oh, dude, you lost some weight. You must have lost some strength. How do you deal with that? I've improved other physical qualities. My one rep max squat bench deadlift is not the only thing that I care about. I think that I'm strong enough. If I was at the pearly gates and God told me that I had to give some strength standards before coming in, these aren't anything to live and die by. These curved treadmills are motorless, they're self-driven, manual, you control the speed by how fast you move your legs. The curve absorbs the impact of your front foot more than running on flat ground will. This reduced impact will put less stress on your lower body, which I've already mentioned but I'll say it again, that is the most important thing to pay attention to when you first start running. Heart rate or heart zones on one, two, three, four, doesn't matter much. The curved treadmill also gives a little bit of feedback or momentum with each stride, whereas when you run on pavement your legs have to do a bit more work to propel you forward. === FILE: STOP Overthinking Your Deadlift - 5 Tips [NDJytDIl8pc].txt ===

Ok, go ahead and do 5 reps. Ok, go ahead and do 5 reps. In this video, I'm going to give you 5 tips that will help you stop overthinking your deadlift setup and stop the unnecessary fidgeting between reps. If it takes you 60 seconds to perform 5 hard reps, pay attention. Number one, don't let go of the bar. Squeeze the bar with your hands for the entire set. Don't relax your grip. The deadlift is a bit different than the other barbell movements because you have the opportunity to fully rest at the bottom. This rest period between reps is opening a window for you to overthink, pause, delay and fidget. Squeezing the bar for the entire set will trick your body into thinking it's bearing the load the whole time without any rest. Number two, perform pause and go reps. You've probably heard of touch and go reps. These are performed by pulling the first rep and then lowering the bar back to the same starting position, tapping the weight on the ground, and going straight into the second rep. This is basically what I want you to do, but I want you to pause the weight on the floor for one second and then go. Get it? Pause and go. This will ensure you are not using any momentum, the plates are bouncing off the platform and the plates are motionless, dead, before lifting the weight. So instead of drop, relax, wiggle your feet around, spirit fingers, run through a checklist in your head, then go, just lower, pause and go. Number three, breathe and brace at the top. Take a deep breath, pull your first rep. Exhale at the top, take a big breath, brace, lower the bar, pause and go. Breathing and bracing at the top means you have one less thing to do at the bottom. Now if you find that you can't hold your breath all the way down and all the way up, lower the barbell faster. If you still need more air, you might be getting fatigued as the set goes on or the rep speed is just really slowing down, a lot of time under tension. You can rapidly breathe and brace at the bottom too. Number four, let gravity pull the bar down. This isn't meant to be an instructional deadlift video, so I'll be brief. Lower the bar in the same path that you picked it up, a straight line, hips first, knees second. Imagine the barbell weighs 1,000 pounds and you were tasked with lowering it under control. Gravity is going to pull the bar straight down. You aren't going to be able to push it around your knees, drop it a few inches from your shins because you don't want the bar to scrape your supermodel legs. No, it's going to go straight down. Let the barbell drop straight down and pull you back into the correct starting position. Imagine that you were doing a Smith machine deadlift. The bar can only travel up and down in a straight line. Your skeleton will self-organize on the way down. Number five, move the barbell. That's right, move the barbell. Not on the first rep, but on the subsequent reps. If you don't follow tip number four and you drop the barbell in a different spot, just set up front of the knees, flush with the front of the arms, then roll the barbell to your shins. On rep one, you set up to the barbell. On rep two and beyond, set the barbell up to you. Stop chasing the bar each rep by shuffling your feet around the platform. I understand if you have hexagonal plates, there's not a great way around this. In this case, it's going to be even more important to control the weight as you lower it. IMight actually perform controlled touch-and-go reps in this scenario. Now, if you're deadlifting on a very damaged platform, maybe it's time to change the platform if it's yours, or you can use some rubber mats under the plates and your feet to minimize the dents. One advantage to walking lunges over split squats, or Bulgarian split squats, is balance is much less of a limiting factor. If you've done Bulgarian split squats before, you know that balance is the most difficult part, and the fatigue that comes from stabilizing your front leg will force you to stop before the big muscles actually fail. During walking lunges, you get to bring your feet together at the start and completion of every rep. Resetting your balance and taking a very brief rest at the top, similar to the rest at the top of a squat. This allows me to push my legs during walking lunges without feeling like I'm competing in a survivor challenge, and without jumping my front foot around like hopscotch. Don't get me wrong, split squats and Bulgarian split squats are a fine movement. If you enjoy doing them, go ahead and continue doing them. For walking lunges, the most common mistake I see is people treating the lunge like a lunge stretch. We're not trying to stretch, we're trying to build muscle. Now obviously, all weight trening movements stretch the muscle under load, but we aren't looking for maximum range of motion or maximum stride length. Your stride length actually doesn't matter to an extent. It's thought that a longer stride will target your glute muscles more than a shorter stride, but I get plenty of muscle fatigue and soreness in my glutes without exaggerating my stride length. You need to lunge only to a length that allows your front foot to stay flat, back knee down to the ground, and back foot heel raised. This works. It doesn't need to look like this. In fact, it shouldn't. Maximum stride length severely limits the amount of weight you can use because you can't apply very much force up. Your feet are pushing to the front and back. And in order to recover out of this position, you have to lean forward. If you're unable to keep your front foot flat and your heel lifts off the ground, your lunge length, stride length might be a little bit too short. Instead, lunge forward and place your front foot flat on the ground. Drop your back knee straight down to the ground. Let your back heel lift off the ground. You should try to let your knee travel forward over your toes. This will use a little morEQuads than if your knee is behind your toes or heels. As you stand up, stand straight up. Think about moving the dumbbells up in a straight line. Do not swing your upper body forward. Do not swing the weight forward. The middle section of the lunge should resemble a stationary split squat, up and down. As you lower your back knee to the ground, do it under control. Do not slam your knee to the ground. Think of the eccentric of each lunge as equally important as the concentric portion. The down is as important as the up. So don't skip it by pile driving your knee into the ground. Take your time with these. Don't rush through them as fast as possible. Don't start the next lunge before fully completing the previous lunge. You can do these with a barbell or dumbbells. I like the extra isometric stretch on the traps with the dumbbell lunges. And it's easier to set up. Which is why they have been my lunge of choice lately. If you find that your grip is giving out, you can use a bar on your back. Or you can use straps on your dumbbell lunges. Yes, as non-hardcore as that sounds, you can use straps for dumbbell lunges. Now fast forward to current times, 2025, and I'd like to give an update on the status of the high bar back squat versus the low bar back squat. I'm just going to spoil the video now and say that I don't really teach the high bar squat or the low bar squat anymore. I just teach the squat. As a coach or personal trener, trying to pigeonhole lifters into camp high bar or low bar is actually a sign of only understanding something on a surface level. You've memorized how to high bar squat. Bar on top of your traps, vertical torso, head and chest straight ahead, sit down without leaning forward, stand up the same way. You've memorized how to low bar squat. Bar across the spine of your scapula, bend over, head and chest down, hips back on the way down, hip drive on the way up. You've basically memorized a script, and if you're lucky, the lifter that you're coaching fits the script, and you're both happy. Personally, in the past, sometimes it didn't work out like that, and when I'm coaching someone, something just seemed off with their squat, but I would hesitate to make a correction if it crossed the line of high bar squat to low bar squat. I was coaching the squat with my hands tied because I was essentially just coaching the high bar squat or the low bar squat rather than coaching the lifter. And I was starting to feel like I cared more about the aesthetics of their low bar squat or of their high bar squat rather than just worrying about their squat in general. Dudes would come to me, and they'd say they want to squat more weight, and I'd take a look at their technique. They would display a perfect high bar squat, and my go-mad brain would say, well, if you want to squat more weight, you need to learn how to low bar squat. When the solution wasn't any sort of adjustment to their technique, it might have just been a program adjustment, or most of the time it was definitely just you need more time under the bar. They care more about you following the program to a T than becoming a more self-sufficient lifter. You need to do your three sets of five. You need to add five pounds each session. When you fail to add five pounds, reduce the weight by 15% and work your way back up. If you fail again, repeat the process. If you fail a third time, you're not sleeping enough, you're not eating enough, or you're just being a pussy. This is a classic example of a coach caring more about the program than actually helping the lifter. And this is sort of how I felt about coaching the high bar squat and the low bar squat. I was more concerned with them hitting these technique bullet points than just worrying about the results they were getting. I should be helping them squat in whatever way needed to squat hard and squat often. I don't need to analyze their squat to determine if they're a high bar squatter or a low bar squatter. In my most recent how to squat video, which is still a few years old, I talk about the three pillars of a good squat. So if you were to ask me, how does my squat look? The firsT3 things that I'm going to look for. Number one, the lifter is balanced on their feet. Number two, the lifter is squatting to depth. And number three, there are no drastic changes in their back angle. Key word here is drastic. === FILE: The Lifting Community & Running Community have the same problem. [-KqKEf7vtEk].txt ===

 Hey everyone, my name is Alan Thrall, I like lifting weights, and I somewhat recently got into running. I try not to spend too much time on social media, but even still, I've noticed that some of the running community does a lot of the same stuff that the lifting community does a lot of the same stuff that the lifting community does, stuff that kind of annoys me. Number one, they both worry too much about their technique looking a certain way. I've already talked about this at length for lifters, but some runners do the same thing. Don't run like this, red X, run like this, green X, and check mark. I'm all for the same thing, green X, and check mark. I'm all for sharing tips and helpful technique cues. I'm not saying that running and lifting technique does not matter. Being efficient and moving weight or running is a good thing. But I do roll my eyes when people worry so much about their technique needing to look a certain way, or content creators who tell you to look a certain way. We are all different individuals with different heights, weights, anthropometry, limb length, gait, stride length, footfall, posture, and so much more. You might be a tall, lanky person with heavy feet and choppy stride. You might be a petite, compact person who glides across the asphalt like a gazelle. Your long legs and short torso might require a lot of bending over during a full depth squat. Or you might effortlessly high bar squat with a perfectly vertical torso up and down like a piston. None of these things are right or wrong. And my point is, we are all built differently and we tend to move accordingly. We are adaptable creatures and we become accustomed to the way we've moved our whole life. I am especially bothered by runners who make bold claims like, you have shin splints because you run like this, red X. Your knees hurt because you have poor running posture, red X. Blaming the cause of pain on purely mechanical reasons. You're probably experiencing pain because you're running too many miles, too fast, too soon. Not because your arms swing across your body instead of front to back. Number two, worrying too much about the minor details of scheduling. Should I run before a weight trening session or after? Can I run and do a lower body weight trening session on the same day? Should I have one day off between my runs and my squat session? These sound a lot like, should I squat or deadlift first? Can I squat and deadlift on the same day? How many days of rest should I have between squats and deadlifts? The number one answer to all of thesEQuestions, running or lifting, whatever you prefer. What works best with your schedule? What feels better for you? Run first, lift second? Lift first, run second? You are probably not going to affect your results positively or negatively by switching around your workouts. Your routine should be what's easiest to stick with. Personally, I find it easier to go on a run first thing in the morning than it is to get ready and go to the gym and lift. That's why I do it. I've enjoyed upper body weight trening sessions on the same days as my run because they're usually shorter than lower body sessions. I like lower body sessions on my non-running days because I feel best and have more time that way. It comes down to personal preference and scheduling. There was a few months where the best time for my run during the day was on my way to the gym. So I'd run to the gym, do my squats, and then I'd run or bike home if my bike was at the gym. What are you emphasizing? Are you trening for a powerlifting meet? Then running should be on the back burner and you should probably lift weights whenever you feel best and have the most time. Are you trening for a race? You should probably devote your running workouts to the days when you have the most energy, most time, and least amount of stress. Lifting is on the back burner. It needs to be done, but it's not a priority. Fit your workouts in according to your personal schedule and preference. You can't go wrong in that way. And number three, worrying too much about progression. I gotta lift more weight than last week. I gotta do more reps. I gotta run more miles. I gotta run faster. I need to progressively overload in order to make progress. You can run the same distance at the same pace week after week or even slower. You can lift the same weight for the same reps week after week or even less. Add weight or increase pace and mileage when you feel comfortable or when the same thing starts requiring less effort. You don't need to overload yourself by always stressing about doing more, especially when you are doing more and it feels harder. We become attracted to doing more because it makes us think that we are getting better. But if we do more and it's harder, it doesn't necessarily mean we are improving. Barbell Medicine talks about using the term progressive loading rather than progressive overloading in their podcast. I'd highly suggest checking that out. I hope this video didn't come off as negative. I'm trying to do the opposite by encouraging you not to fret if your running technique is a little sloppy. Plan your running and lifting sessions in a way that fits your schedule. And go slow. If you do it for long enough, you'll get better. Thanks for watching and always remember, TREAD ON TIME!

My point is that it's not just always a lack of willpower. While it is up to you to take control of your situation, it is easier for some and more difficult for others. === FILE: We have been LIED to - Bodybuilding & Powerlifting [0yUZ5pb7UA0].txt ===

 Once upon a time there was bodybuilding, bodybuilding, bodybuilding, bodybuilding was a way to build your body and mind through the use of weights and calisthenic exercises. One day bodybuilding meant powerlifting. They both had a lot in common and decided to get married. They would basically finish each other's sentences. Lowering the bar resembles a controlled drop straight down to the floor and you are just going along for the ride while resisting gravity. In other words, you aren't getting into a great starting position on rep number one because you have no tactile feedback. rep number one, the bar is pulling you into a better starting position for rep number two. I would suggest paying close attention to any deviations and differences between your starting position on rep number one and subsequent reps. Even if you lower the weight quickly, and even if you pause the weight on the ground, your body is still locked and loaded, ready to pop the weight back up. This is the reason why some people use a dynamic start when deadlifting. It can just be something as simple as a quick pop of the hips up and down. Doing this is a way to use a tiny bit of stretch reflex in the lower body before pulling the weight off the ground. It's a concerted effort to load your muscles and joints before pulling the weight from a dead stop. === FILE: ＂I can't keep my BACK TIGHT on Deadlifts＂ [dVPZDeCDwEc].txt ===

Hey everyone, I'm Alan Thrall here at Untamed Strength Gym in Sacramento, California. I want to show you a few different approaches for fixing a round back deadlift. You might be said round back deadlifter, or maybe you're a coach or a trener and your client has this problem. A few things first. Number one, these drills are meant for someone who can't set their back or keep their back tight on any reps. I'm not talking about a power lifter who's back only rounds over at maximum weights. Again, it's for people who don't have the kinesthetic understanding or the body awareness that's required to keep your back flat or tight. Number two, a little bit of backgrounding is fine. I don't say this to be contrarian. I'm not putting out a blanket statement like technique doesn't matter. I'm saying this because there's some truth to it. When I say a little bit of backgrounding is fine. Your spine is meant to flex and extend. A lot of very strong people purposely do this under load to strengthen their back. I don't want you to be afraid of lifting weights because your back rounds a little bit. I don't want you to suffer from paralysis by analysis and overanalyze everything about lifting weights. Number three, rolling off of point number two, a little bit of backgrounding is fine, especially if it's dosed correctly. Your tissues adapt to the stress you place on them. If you start light and you're smart about adding weight, you'll most likely be fine. But if you consistently max out your tissues every week past their capacity, you're increasing the likelihood of injury. This is why I'm not overly concerned with beginners who struggled to keep their back flat while dead lifting. They're using light weights and their tissues can handle those light weights. They're learning. So it's okay as you learn and get stronger. A go hard lifter who's consistently maxing out each week with ugly form is more of a concern to me. They're starting to flirt with loads that are over their capacity. And number four, your flat back might look different than my flat back. Some people have naturally more or less curve in their spine. You can observe this just by looking at people's natural posture. So if natural resting posture varies, deadlift starting positions will also vary. When I'm coaching a beginner, I like to tell them to stick their chest out proud, usually towards the ground a few feet in front of them. Put wrinkles in the back of your shirt. That end product might be more or less extended from person to person. So wherever you start, try to hold that same position as you pull the weight. I don't want to see immediate rounding and loss of tightness as you pull. This means the muscles that you're trying to tren aren't doing the best job that they could. I want those muscles to work hard so they can get stronger. Your back is trying to remain rigid. So the force you generate from your legs can trensfer through your back and into the barbell. It's sort of like getting really tight before descending on a squat only to dive bomb and fold over as you stand up. You're not holding a strong position throughout the movement and I want to fix that. Try these corrections that I'm about to list and see which ones work best. I have placed them in order that I would use if I was to triage this issue, but you can use whatever order you'd like. You can also use a combination of these steps to achieve what you're looking for. Number one, toes out, knees out. This is nice and simple and very quick pointing your toes out and pushing your knees out against your arms might be just enough to create some space between your front porch and the top of your thighs. Having this extra space allows you to extend your back, which extends the front of your body too. If your toes and knees are straightforward, you might feel like the top of your thighs are pushing your guts in, which rounds your lower back once you begin to pull. Number two, ditch the belt. If you are wearing a belt when you deadlift and you can't maintain back tightness, especially lower back tightness, the belt might be making things worse. It's ironic that some people use a belt to help keep their back tight, but it only ends up making it harder for you to keep your back tight and your midsection braced. If a belt is worn too tight or too low, or the belt itself is just too thick or it's too wide, it can actually push your guts in. This coupled with bending over to grab the bar causes your stomach to be pushed in by the top of your thighs. Just like I talked about with point number one. For some people wearing a belt for deadlifts is not as comfortable as it is for squats. This is usually because your squat stance is wider and your torso might be a little bit more vertical, but when you deadlift, your stance is narrower and you probably have to bend over more to grab the bar. Here's some power lifting knowledge. Some of the best squatters in the world are very stocky and thick waisted because that helps when you squat, but their deadlift is quite a bit lower than their squat because that stocky thick waist is usually a disadvantage in the deadlift. And some of the best deadlifters in the world are what people would call thin wasted deadlifters, maybe a lanky type. I've noticed that people who lose a noticeable amount of body weight tend to maintain their deadlift strength pretty well because the starting position actually feels better without extra weight around the midsection. And this all just illustrates that a belt increases your waist circumference, which might work against you. Keyword here is might. This is only a problem for a minority of people. Deadlifts without a belt feel better than deadlifts with a belt for some people. Number three, set your back at the top. Rather than trying to set your back in a good position after grabbing the barbell when you're already bent over, try getting your back tight at the top. As you descend, keep your arms straight, pointing down, push your hips back and only bend your knees enough to let them travel into the insides of your arms. Do not let them pass in front of your arms. Once you can put your hands on the barbell, grab it and go. Keeping that same position as you pull. Number four, touch and go deadlifts. Now that you're at the top, keep that position as you lower the bar back down to the floor. Pause on the floor without losing tightness, without losing any tension, then pull the next rep. At the top, keep that position, lower the bar by pushing your hips back, sliding the bar down your legs, pause on the floor, stand back up. Now most people do a controlled drop at the top of a deadlift and this is fine if you have no problem resetting each rep. If you're struggling to get tight against the bar, you can perform these touch and go reps. I put touch and go in quotes because it's not a touch and go deadlift where you just barely tap the ground or where you slam the bar against the ground and use momentum to carry you through to the next rep. I want the plates to fully touch the ground, fully deload on the ground. You'll pause then perform your next rep, staying tight the entire set, holding your position the entire set. Number five, tempo. One unique difference between the deadlift and the squat and bench is the fact that the deadlift does not start with an eccentric or a lengthening or a loading portion. It starts with a concentric effort. For beginners, this makes getting tight before the lift even more difficult. Some lifters go from zero to a hundred miles per hour, no tension to maximum effort. And during this explosive effort, they lose any tension that they might've had before the bar left the floor. It's not a matter of just getting tight. It's getting tight against the bar. Pulling slowly throughout the entire movement might give them time to focus on keeping their back tight. I like to suggest holding your back isometrically then pushing with the legs. Again, slowing down gives the lifter more time to think and more time to contemplate why they are voluntarily subjecting themselves to this torture. The slow motion pull should be exactly that slow motion. The speed should not change throughout the movement. I would suggest using a tempo on the way up and down. Number six, a block pull. Block pull refers to propping the weight up so that the bar is at a higher starting position. Standard plates on the floor will result in about a nine inch bar height. My suggestion is to use blocks to raise the bar to anywhere between 12 to 15 inches is pretty common. You can also use wagon wheels or do rack pulls where you use the safeties in a squat rack to raise the barbell plates, not even touching the ground, but beware this can damage the bar. If you're using a lot of weight, sometimes the bar is just too low for a lifters current mobility. Raising the barbell will meet the lifter where they're at. Try to find at what height the lifter has to start rounding over at the back in order to reach the bar, then prop the weight up just above that. Over time you can try lowering the start height. Number seven, sumo deadlift. Contrary to popular belief, the sumo deadlift is not much different than a conventional deadlift in terms of muscles used, muscle activation and range of motion. The difference between sumo and conventional is about as much as the difference between your normal moderate grip bench press and a close grip bench press. Maybe not even that. The extreme conventional deadlift with the heels touching versus the extreme sumo deadlift with toes out to the plates is where the differences become very noticeable. But if your grip remains the same and you just move your feet just inside of your hands or just outside of your hands, it has minimal impact on your hip height and your starting position. The narrow stance sumo deadlift might free up some space for your front porch. Your stomach won't be pushed in by the top of your thighs, which should allow more space for you to set your back. Number eight, Romanian deadlift. Last but not least, if things are just not clicking, you might just do Romanian deadlifts for a few weeks or a few months. The Romanian deadlift combines a number of the steps I just listed. It starts at the top, ends at the top. You use a tempo on the descent as you lower the bar and you can perform touch and go reps. When performing the Romanian deadlift, use the same stance and grip that you would use for deadlifts from the floor. Push your hips back throughout the entire movement. Never let your hips drop down. Think hips back, not down. Knees should be unlocked, not hyperextended, but they should not move forward. You are not actively bending your knees as you lower the bar. Keep your knees behind your arms. That's it. Thanks for watching and always remember, TRY NOW TIME!
